title: Peleus apud Ceycem
titleEn: The Hawk and the Wolf — Metamorphoses XI.266–409
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Peleus, guilty of a brother's blood and driven from his father's house, comes as a suppliant to Trachis, where Ceyx rules without force or bloodshed and is himself in mourning for a brother. Asked why he weeps, Ceyx tells of that brother, Daedalion, whose daughter Chione bore twins to two gods, set herself above Diana and was shot through the tongue for it; Daedalion threw himself from Parnassus, and Apollo caught him up as a hawk that now rages at every bird. Before the tale is finished a herdsman runs up with word that a wolf is tearing Peleus's herds on the shore, and Peleus, taking the losses for a dead man's due, prays to the bereaved Nereid until the beast is fixed in marble at the neck of a torn heifer.

advisory.lede: At XI.306–310 two gods rape Chione: Mercury by force while she lies drugged asleep, and Apollo that night in the disguise of an old woman.
advisory.more: Apollo puts off his hope until nightfall; Mercury will not wait. He touches the girl's face with the wand that brings on sleep, and while she lies under that touch she suffers the god's force — vimque dei patitur, the plain Latin for rape. Night comes on, and Apollo counterfeits an old woman and takes the pleasure already snatched before him. The Latin gives her age, at XI.302, as twice seven years. The translation keeps the violence of vim patitur and softens nothing. The rest of the part is violent in other ways — the same girl is later shot through the tongue by Diana, her father throws himself from a cliff, a wolf tears a herd on the shore — but the text does not stop to dwell on the wounds, and the whole of it is presented unaltered.

sentences.t:
Felix et nato, felix et coniuge Peleus
et cui, si demas iugulati crimina Phoci,
omnia contigerant.
sentences.l: Happy both in his son and happy in his wife, Peleus, and one to whom, if you take away the charge of Phocus with his throat cut, all things had fallen out.
sentences.i: Peleus was happy both in his son and in his wife — a man to whom everything had come, if you subtract the guilt of Phocus's murder.
sentences.n: et ... et here is the doubled correlative, “both ... and”, tying the two ablatives of respect nato and coniuge. The relative cui is dative and hangs on contigerant, “had fallen to him”; demas is a potential subjunctive with an indefinite “you”, “if one were to take away”. iugulati Phoci is an objective genitive — the charge is not Phocus's but the charge concerning him, and iugulatus names the manner: his throat was cut.

sentences.t:
Fraterno sanguine sontem
expulsumque domo patria Trachinia tellus
accipit.
sentences.l: Him, guilty by a brother's blood and driven out from his father's home, the Trachinian land receives.
sentences.i: The land of Trachis takes him in — guilty of a brother's blood, and thrown out of his father's house.
sentences.n: sontem and expulsum are both accusative, the object of accipit; the subject Trachinia tellus is held to the end of 269 and the verb accipit opens 270. Fraterno sanguine is the ablative of the charge with sontem, “guilty by a brother's blood”, and domo patria an ablative of separation with expulsum.

sentences.t:
Hic regnum sine vi, sine caede regebat
Lucifero genitore satus patriumque nitorem
ore ferens Ceyx, illo qui tempore maestus
dissimilisque sui fratrem lugebat ademptum.
sentences.l: Here Ceyx was ruling the kingdom without force, without slaughter — sown from the Lightbringer as father, and carrying his father's brightness in his face — who at that time, mournful and unlike himself, was grieving for a brother taken away.
sentences.i: Here Ceyx ruled without force and without bloodshed — begotten of the Morning Star, and wearing his father's brightness in his face; at that time he was in mourning and not like himself, grieving for a brother taken from him.
sentences.n: The subject Ceyx does not arrive until the third line of the sentence: regebat comes first at 270, then two participial phrases, satus “sown, begotten” with the ablative Lucifero genitore, and ferens; only at 272 does the name appear. Lucifer is the morning star, and patrium nitorem is his light passed down into his son's face. sui is the genitive of the reflexive with dissimilis, “unlike himself”.

sentences.t:
Quo postquam Aeacides fessus curaque viaque
venit et intravit paucis comitantibus urbem,
quosque greges pecorum, quae secum armenta trahebat,
haud procul a muris sub opaca valle reliquit,
sentences.l: And to that place, after the descendant of Aeacus, weary both with care and with the road, came and entered the city with few accompanying, and what flocks of sheep, what herds he was driving with him, he left not far from the walls under a shady valley,
sentences.i: When the Aeacid came there, worn out by worry and by the road, and entered the city with only a few companions, and left the flocks and herds he was driving with him in a shady valley not far from the walls —
sentences.n: Quo is the connecting relative used as an adverb of place, “and to there”, with postquam following it. Aeacides is a patronymic, “descendant of Aeacus”; the man is Peleus, named at 266 and addressed by name at 284. paucis comitantibus is an ablative absolute with a present participle, “with a few accompanying”. quosque greges and quae armenta are relative-adjective clauses with their nouns drawn inside them, “what flocks he was driving, those he left”. This unit ends at a comma because the sentence has no stop at all until 281.

sentences.t:
copia cum facta est adeundi prima tyranni,
velamenta manu praetendens supplice, qui sit
se quoque satus, memorat, tantum sua crimina celat
mentiturque fugae causam:
sentences.l: when the first chance of approaching the ruler had been made, holding out woollen bands with suppliant hand, he tells who he is and from whom he is sprung; only, he hides his own crimes and lies about the cause of his flight:
sentences.i: when his first chance came to approach the king, stretching out the woollen bands in a suppliant's hand, he told who he was and whose son — only, he kept his own crimes hidden and lied about why he had fled:
sentences.n: copia ... adeundi ... tyranni is the gerundive in the genitive, tyranni adeundi, “of the ruler to be approached”, which is Latin's way of saying “the opportunity of approaching the ruler”; prima stands between the two words. supplice agrees with manu across two words, “with a suppliant hand”. The archive prints se at the head of 280; se is accusative and satus nominative, so the two cannot agree, and the second witness omits the word, leaving the two indirect questions qui sit and quo-que satus [sit], which is how the literal takes it. That quoque is the trap: it is quo plus the enclitic -que, “and from whom”, not the adverb “also”. tantum is adverbial, “only, except that”.

sentences.t:
petit, urbe vel agro
se iuvet.
sentences.l: he asks: let him help him with a city or with land.
sentences.i: he asked the king to help him — with a place in the town, or with land.
sentences.n: petit takes a subjunctive without ut, the paratactic construction, “he asks: let him help”. urbe and agro are ablatives of means with iuvet. se is the reflexive in an indirect command and looks back to the subject of petit, Peleus — the man asking, not the king asked.

sentences.t:
Hunc contra placido Trachinius ore
talibus adloquitur:
sentences.l: The Trachinian, in reply, with a calm face, addresses this man with such words:
sentences.i: The Trachinian answered him with a calm face, and spoke like this:
sentences.n: contra here is the adverb, “in reply, in answer”, not a preposition governing Hunc, which is simply the object of adloquitur. Trachinius, “the man of Trachis”, is Ceyx, named at 272. talibus is a bare ablative with adloquitur and has no noun of its own: “with such words” is supplied from the sense.

sentences.t:
“Mediae quoque commoda plebi
nostra patent, Peleu, nec inhospita regna tenemus.
sentences.l: “Our good things lie open to the middling common people too, Peleus, and we do not hold an inhospitable kingdom.
sentences.i: “What we have stands open even to ordinary folk, Peleus; the kingdom we hold is not one that turns strangers away.
sentences.n: quoque here is the adverb “too”, and it belongs with mediae plebi: even the middling sort. commoda nostra is neuter plural, “our advantages, our resources”, and patent is “stand open”. regna is a poetic plural for the one kingdom. inhospita denies exactly the duty a suppliant comes to claim.

sentences.t:
Adicis huic animo momento potentia, clarum
nomen avumque Iovem.
sentences.l: You are adding to this willingness, by weight, powerful things — a bright name, and Jupiter for a grandfather.
sentences.i: And to that willingness of mine you add, with weight behind them, powerful things: a famous name, and Jupiter for a grandfather.
sentences.n: The archive prints momento, an ablative singular; potentia is the neuter plural of potens and is then left with no noun to agree with, and the accusatives clarum nomen avumque Iovem stand in apposition to it. The second witness reads momenta, neuter plural, “weighty inducements”, which potentia fits exactly. The literal follows the printed momento as a bare ablative, “by weight”. huic animo is Ceyx's own goodwill, the thing being added to.

sentences.t:
Ne tempora perde precando!
Quod petis, omne feres tuaque haec pro parte vocato,
qualiacumque vides! Utinam meliora videres!'
sentences.l: Do not waste time by asking! What you seek, all of it you will carry off, and call these things here yours, for your share, of whatever sort you see them! Would that you saw better ones!”
sentences.i: Don't waste time asking! Whatever you ask for, you will have it all; take what is here for your share and call it yours, such as you see it. I only wish you had better to look at.”
sentences.n: ne perde is a negative command with the plain imperative, an older and more emphatic turn than noli perdere. vocato is the future imperative, “call, and go on calling”. Utinam with the imperfect subjunctive videres is a wish about the present that is not so, and it plays on the vides that ends the sentence before it — the same verb twice on 288, the second time in a mood that admits the thing cannot happen. The archive closes this speech at 288 with a single apostrophe where it opened at 283 with a double mark; the mismatch is in the printing and nothing in the wording is affected.

sentences.t:
Et flebat: moveat tantos quae causa dolores,
Peleusque comitesque rogant. Quibus ille profatur:
sentences.l: And he was weeping: what cause moves such great griefs, both Peleus and his companions ask. And to them he speaks out:
sentences.i: And he was weeping. Peleus and his companions ask what cause stirs such grief; and he says to them:
sentences.n: moveat is subjunctive in an indirect question, and the question stands in front of rogant, the verb that governs it. Peleusque comitesque is the doubled -que, “both ... and”. Quibus is a connecting relative opening its sentence, “and to them”, not a question word.

sentences.t:
“Forsitan hanc volucrem, rapto quae vivit et omnes
terret aves, semper pennas habuisse putetis:
sentences.l: “Perhaps you may suppose that this bird, which lives on what it snatches and terrifies all birds, has always had feathers:
sentences.i: “Perhaps you think this bird — the one that lives by robbery and frightens every other bird — has always had wings:
sentences.n: forsitan takes the subjunctive putetis, “you may perhaps suppose”. The accusative and infinitive hanc volucrem ... habuisse is the content of the supposing, and the relative clause quae vivit et terret is packed inside it, between the accusative and its infinitive. rapto is a neuter participle used as a noun in the ablative, “on what has been snatched”, the regular way of saying “by plunder”.

sentences.t:
vir fuit et (tanta est animi constantia!) iam tum
acer erat belloque ferox ad vimque paratus,
nomine Daedalion.
sentences.l: He was a man, and — so great is the steadiness of a nature! — even then he was fierce, and savage in war, and ready for violence, Daedalion by name.
sentences.i: He was a man once; and — such is the persistence of a nature! — even then he was fierce, wild in war, ready for violence. Daedalion was his name.
sentences.n: The parenthesis is in the present tense inside a past narrative: tanta est, “so great is”, because the point holds now, of the bird. animi constantia is the constancy of a disposition, the thing that survives the change of body. nomine is an ablative of respect, “by name”, and the name is held to the very end of the sentence.

sentences.t:
Illo genitore creatis,
qui vocat auroram caeloque novissimus exit,
(cura mihi pax est) pacis mihi cura tenendae
coniugiique fuit, fratri fera bella placebant:
sentences.l: To us begotten from that father — who calls the dawn and goes out of the sky last — (peace is my care) the care of peace to be kept and of marriage was mine; fierce wars pleased my brother:
sentences.i: We were sons of that father who calls up the dawn and is the last to leave the sky. For my part — peace is what I care about — my care was the keeping of peace and of a marriage; my brother liked savage war.
sentences.n: Illo genitore creatis is a dative plural covering both brothers, and the sentence then splits it in two, mihi ... fuit and fratri ... placebant. The father is Lucifer, described by what he does rather than named. pacis tenendae is a gerundive genitive with cura, “the care of peace to be kept”, and coniugii is a second genitive under the same cura. The parenthesis restates in the present what the clause around it says in the past; where the archive prints cura there, the second witness reads culta, “peace has been tended by me”.

sentences.t:
illius virtus reges gentesque subegit,
quae nunc Thisbaeas agitat mutata columbas.
sentences.l: His manhood subdued kings and peoples — which now, changed, harries the doves of Thisbe.
sentences.i: That courage of his brought kings and nations under him; and now, changed, it hunts the doves of Thisbe.
sentences.n: The relative quae picks up virtus, a feminine noun, not the man himself: it is the courage that is said to have been changed and to hunt now, and mutata is a perfect participle agreeing with quae. Thisbaeas is an adjective made from a place-name, marking the doves by where they come from.

sentences.t:
Nata erat huic Chione. Quae dotatissima forma
mille procos habuit, bis septem nubilis annis.
sentences.l: A daughter had been born to him, Chione. She, most richly dowered as to beauty, had a thousand suitors, marriageable at twice seven years.
sentences.i: He had a daughter, Chione. Most richly dowered with beauty, she had a thousand suitors, of an age to marry at fourteen.
sentences.n: Nata erat huic is the dative of the person concerned with a verb of being born, “there had been born to him”, Latin's ordinary way of saying he had a daughter. dotatissima forma is a superlative with an ablative of respect, “most dowered as to her looks”: her beauty is the dowry. bis septem annis is an ablative of time, and Latin counts the number out rather than saying fourteen. nubilis is the technical word for a girl of an age to be married.

sentences.t:
Forte revertentes Phoebus Maiaque creatus,
ille suis Delphis, hic vertice Cylleneo,
videre hanc pariter, pariter traxere calorem.
sentences.l: By chance, returning, Phoebus and the one begotten of Maia — that one from his own Delphi, this one from the Cyllenian peak — saw her at the same time, at the same time drew in heat.
sentences.i: As it happened, Phoebus and Maia's son were both on their way back — the one from his own Delphi, the other from the peak of Cyllene — and they saw her at the same moment, and at the same moment caught fire.
sentences.n: videre and traxere are the third-plural perfects for viderunt and traxerunt, the poetic -ere for -erunt; they are the only finite verbs in the sentence and both stand in 305. Maia creatus is a periphrasis for Mercury, “he begotten of Maia”, matched by Phoebus for Apollo. ille and hic distribute the two in the order they were just named. calorem traxere is “drew in heat”, the physical word used of falling in love. Magnus prints calorem, “heat”, the fire of desire; some editions print colorem, which would have the two draw colour instead.

sentences.t:
Spem veneris differt in tempora noctis Apollo,
non fert ille moras virgaque movente soporem
virginis os tangit:
sentences.l: Apollo puts off the hope of love-making into the hours of night; that other one does not bear delays, and with the wand that stirs up sleep he touches the girl's face:
sentences.i: Apollo puts off his hope of her until nightfall; the other will not put up with waiting, and touches the girl's face with the wand that brings on sleep:
sentences.n: veneris here is the common noun, “love-making, sex”, not the goddess. ille means the other of the two, Mercury, who was the hic of 304 — the pronoun switches because the point of view has moved. virga movente soporem is an ablative of means with a present participle inside it, “with the wand causing sleep”. tangit is a historic present, and the narrative runs in the present from here.

sentences.t:
tactu iacet illa potenti
vimque dei patitur.
sentences.l: at that powerful touch she lies still, and suffers the god's force.
sentences.i: under that powerful touch she lies helpless, and suffers the god's violence.
sentences.n: tactu ... potenti is an ablative of cause, with the adjective potenti held to the end of 308, away from its noun at the start of the phrase. vim patitur is the plain Latin for being raped: vis is force, and patior is what is done to a person, not what a person does; patitur is deponent, passive in form but with she as its subject. Both layers keep the word force, because there is no gentler word in the Latin: she has been put to sleep and cannot resist.

sentences.t:
Nox caelum sparserat astris:
Phoebus anum simulat praereptaque gaudia sumit.
sentences.l: Night had strewn the sky with stars: Phoebus counterfeits an old woman and takes joys already snatched before him.
sentences.i: Night had strewn the sky with stars: Phoebus passes himself off as an old woman and takes the pleasure that had already been snatched ahead of him.
sentences.n: praerepta is the perfect participle of praeripio, “snatched away in front of another”: the pleasure has been taken once already, by Mercury, and Apollo takes it after him. simulat with a plain accusative is “counterfeits, passes himself off as” — the old woman is the disguise that gets him in. The pluperfect sparserat sets the hour, and simulat and sumit are historic presents.

sentences.t:
Ut sua maturus complevit tempora venter,
alipedis de stirpe dei versuta propago
nascitur, Autolycus, furtum ingeniosus ad omne,
candida de nigris et de candentibus atra
qui facere adsuerat, patriae non degener artis;
sentences.l: When the ripened womb had filled its own times, from the stock of the wing-footed god a crafty offspring is born, Autolycus, clever for every theft, who had grown used to making white things out of black ones and black out of shining ones, no falling-off from his father's craft;
sentences.i: When the womb came to term and filled out its months, a cunning offspring was born of the wing-footed god's stock: Autolycus, ingenious at every kind of theft, who had made a habit of turning black into white and white into black — no falling-off from his father's art;
sentences.n: sua tempora is the full term, and maturus venter the ripened womb that fills it: Latin puts the ripeness on the belly rather than on the time. alipedis dei is a periphrasis, “the wing-footed god”, Mercury again. ingeniosus takes ad with the accusative for the thing one is clever at. The two colour-phrases are set crosswise — object then de-phrase in candida de nigris, de-phrase then object in de candentibus atra — and the relative qui that governs them stands after both, at the head of 315. degener with the genitive artis is “falling short of” an inherited skill, and the negative turns it into praise.

sentences.t:
nascitur e Phoebo (namque est enixa gemellos)
carmine vocali clarus citharaque Philammon.
sentences.l: There is born from Phoebus — for she had brought forth twins — Philammon, famous for sung song and for the lyre.
sentences.i: And from Phoebus was born — for she bore twins — Philammon, famous for song and for the lyre.
sentences.n: nascitur is repeated from 313, three lines back, and the repetition is what binds the two births into one pair. The parenthesis explains why one birth has two fathers. carmine and cithara are ablatives of respect with clarus, “famous in respect of song and lyre”, and vocali marks the song as sung rather than played. enixa est is the deponent perfect of enitor, “she bore”: the form looks passive and is not.

sentences.t:
Quid peperisse duos et dis placuisse duobus
et forti genitore et progenitore Tonanti
esse satam prodest? An obest quoque gloria? multis
Offuit, huic certe!
sentences.l: What does it profit to have borne two, and to have pleased two gods, and to have been begotten both from a brave father and from the Thunderer as forefather? Or does glory too do harm? To many it has done harm — to this one certainly!
sentences.i: What good was it to have borne two sons, to have pleased two gods, to have been born of a brave father with the Thunderer for forefather? Or can glory do harm as well? It has harmed many, and it harmed her for certain.
sentences.n: Three infinitives — peperisse, placuisse and satam esse — stand together as the subject of prodest, “what does it profit”. The feminine satam shows that the person meant is the girl, though the Latin supplies no accusative subject for the infinitives at all. Tonanti, “the Thunderer”, is ablative here, in the -i ending a present participle takes once it has hardened into a name, and it goes with progenitore, “as forefather”. The edition begins the new sentence at multis, the last word of its line, in lower case, and then prints Offuit with a capital at the head of the next line; the capital is the printing's, not the mark of a fresh sentence. Magnus prints Tonanti; some editions print nitenti, “the shining one”, which would make the forefather the same god who calls the dawn at 295–296 — the speaker's own father, and so the girl's grandfather.

sentences.t:
Quae se praeferre Dianae
sustinuit faciemque deae culpavit.
sentences.l: And she brought herself to set herself before Diana, and found fault with the goddess's face.
sentences.i: She went so far as to rank herself above Diana and to criticise the goddess's face.
sentences.n: Quae opens the sentence as a connecting relative — “and she”, not a relative clause hanging on what came before. sustinuit with an infinitive is “brought herself to”, “could bear to”, and the verb of endurance is what carries the affront. praeferre puts the person outranked in the dative, Dianae.

sentences.t:
At illi
ira ferox mota est “factis” que “placebimus” inquit.
sentences.l: But for her a fierce anger was set moving, and “by deeds”, she says, “we shall please”.
sentences.i: But fierce anger rose in her, and she said: “By deeds we shall please.”
sentences.n: illi is a dative of the person concerned — “anger was set moving for her”, where English says “her anger rose”. placebimus, “we shall please”, answers the placuisse of the opening question, where the girl “pleased” two gods: the goddess will do her pleasing by deeds instead. The edition prints the enclitic -que as a separate word standing outside the quotation marks — factis” que “placebimus — and it is shipped as printed; the -que belongs to factis and joins the sentence, not the quoted words.

sentences.t:
Nec mora, curvavit cornu nervoque sagittam
impulit et meritam traiecit harundine linguam.
sentences.l: Nor was there delay: she bent the horn, and with the string drove the arrow, and pierced with the shaft the deserving tongue.
sentences.i: No delay: she bent her bow, drove the arrow from the string, and ran the shaft through the tongue that had earned it.
sentences.n: Nec mora is a bare noun with no verb — “and no delay” — a stock way of saying that the next thing followed at once. cornu, “horn”, is the bow named from the stuff it is made of, and nervo, “with the string”, is the ablative of what drives the arrow out. meritam linguam, “the deserving tongue”, lays the guilt on the offending part: the tongue that had earned the shaft.

sentences.t:
Lingua tacet, nec vox temptataque verba sequuntur,
conantemque loqui cum sanguine vita reliquit.
sentences.l: The tongue is silent, and neither voice nor the attempted words follow, and life left her, trying to speak, along with her blood.
sentences.i: The tongue falls silent; no voice, no words she tried for, would come; and as she struggled to speak, life left her along with her blood.
sentences.n: conantem, “trying”, is an accusative participle and the object of reliquit: life leaves her while she is still attempting speech. cum sanguine, “with the blood”, sends blood and life out together — the arrow is through her tongue and she bleeds from the mouth. The present tenses tacet and sequuntur hold the moment open until the perfect reliquit closes it.

sentences.t:
Quo miser amplexus ego tum patriumque dolorem
corde tuli fratrique pio solacia dixi!
sentences.l: With what a heart, wretched, did I then bear the embraces and a father's grief, and speak consolations to my loyal brother!
sentences.i: With what a heart I bore it then, wretch that I was — the embraces, a father's grief — and found words of comfort for my devoted brother!
sentences.n: Magnus prints Quo ... amplexus, and the sentence works as an exclamation: quo ... corde, “with what a heart”, with amplexus a fourth-declension accusative plural, “embraces”, standing beside patrium dolorem: the two things he bore. Some editions print quam ... amplexans, “embracing her”, which makes the dead girl the object and the clasping a participle instead. patrium dolorem is the grief that belongs to a father: the man who laments in the next lines is the brother, and the dead girl is his daughter, so the speaker is carrying his brother's grief in his own heart.

sentences.t:
Quae pater haud aliter quam cautes murmura ponti
accipit et natam delamentatur ademptam.
sentences.l: And these words the father receives no otherwise than a rock receives the murmurs of the sea, and he laments aloud for the daughter taken away.
sentences.i: The father takes those words as a cliff takes the mutterings of the sea, and mourns aloud for the daughter torn from him.
sentences.n: Quae, “which things”, is a connecting relative picking up the solacia, the words of comfort just spoken. One verb serves both halves of the comparison — pater accipit quae, and cautes accipit murmura ponti — the rock's verb left to be supplied from the father's. delamentatur is deponent, passive in form and active in sense, and the de- makes the lamenting one that is carried right through: not “mourns” but “mourns out to the end”.

sentences.t:
Ut vero ardentem vidit, quater impetus illi
in medios fuit ire rogos;
sentences.l: But when he saw her burning, four times there was an impulse for him to go into the middle of the pyres;
sentences.i: But when he saw her burning, four times the urge took him to walk into the middle of the pyre;
sentences.n: impetus illi fuit ire is a dative of the possessor with an infinitive — “there was to him an urge to go” — where English says “he had an urge to go”. ardentem, “burning”, has no noun with it and stands for the girl on her pyre; the Latin does not name her again. rogos is a plural for the one pyre, and medios rogos, “the middle pyres”, is Latin's way of saying “the middle of the pyre”, the adjective doing the work of an English noun.

sentences.t:
quater inde repulsus
concita membra fugae mandat similisque iuvenco
spicula crabronum pressa cervice gerenti,
qua via nulla, ruit.
sentences.l: Four times driven back from there, he commits his roused limbs to flight, and, like a bullock carrying the stings of hornets in his galled neck, where there is no way, he rushes.
sentences.i: Four times thrust back, he gives his racing limbs to flight and, like a young bull carrying hornets' stings in his galled neck, charges where there is no path.
sentences.n: similis takes the dative, iuvenco ... gerenti, “like a bullock carrying”, and the participle waits at the end of the next line for the noun it agrees with. pressa cervice is ablative, the neck where the stings are lodged and which they have galled; pressa is a perfect participle of premo agreeing with cervice, but the phrase is not an ablative absolute — it hangs on gerenti as the place of the carrying, not as a clause of its own. qua via nulla, “where there is no way”, has no verb at all, est being left out as often.

sentences.t:
Iam tum mihi currere visus
plus homine est, alasque pedes sumpsisse putares.
sentences.l: Already then he seemed to me to run more than a man, and you would have thought his feet had taken wings.
sentences.i: Even then he seemed to me to be running beyond a man's running, and you would have thought his feet had put on wings.
sentences.n: plus homine, “more than a man”, is an ablative of comparison after plus, with no quam. putares is an imperfect subjunctive of what an onlooker would have thought — Latin's “you would have said”, addressed to no one in particular. The wings are still only a way of speaking here; they arrive in earnest a few lines later.

sentences.t:
Effugit ergo omnes veloxque cupidine leti
vertice Parnasi potitur.
sentences.l: So he escapes them all and, swift with desire of death, gains the peak of Parnassus.
sentences.i: So he outruns them all and, made swift by his craving for death, takes the summit of Parnassus.
sentences.n: potitur, “gets possession of”, governs the ablative vertice and not an accusative. cupidine leti, “with desire of death”, is the ablative of what makes him swift, and says outright where the running is going before he arrives.

sentences.t:
Miseratus Apollo,
cum se Daedalion saxo misisset ab alto,
fecit avem et subitis pendentem sustulit alis
oraque adunca dedit, curvos dedit unguibus hamos,
virtutem antiquam, maiores corpore vires.
sentences.l: Apollo, having taken pity, when Daedalion had sent himself from the high rock, made him a bird and held him up hanging on sudden wings, and gave him a hooked mouth, gave curved hooks for claws, his old courage, strength greater than his body.
sentences.i: Apollo pitied him, and when Daedalion had thrown himself from the high rock, made him a bird, held him up hovering on wings that came in an instant, gave him a hooked beak, gave curved hooks for talons, his old courage, and strength beyond the size of his body.
sentences.n: Miseratus is a deponent participle, passive in form and active in sense, “having taken pity”. fecit avem is a double accusative with the object left to be understood, “made him a bird”. se misisset, “had sent himself”, is the ordinary Latin for throwing oneself down. dedit stands twice in one line, the second time with no connective, and the two accusatives of the following line, virtutem and vires, hang on it without a verb of their own. maiores corpore vires is an ablative of comparison: strength greater than the body that carries it.

sentences.t:
Et nunc accipiter, nulli satis aequus, in omnes
saevit aves aliisque dolens fit causa dolendi.”
sentences.l: And now a hawk, fair enough to none, he rages against all birds, and, grieving, becomes for others a cause of grieving.”
sentences.i: And now he is a hawk, fair to none, and rages against every bird: in his own grief he becomes the cause of grief for others.”
sentences.n: nulli aequus, “fair to nobody”, and aliis causa, “a cause for others”, are both datives; in omnes aves, “against all birds”, is split around the line-end, with in omnes closing one line and aves following the verb on the next. dolens and dolendi are the same verb twice over, once a participle for what he feels and once a gerund for what he makes others do, and the closing line of the tale turns a grief outward on everything that flies.

sentences.t:
Quae dum Lucifero genitus miracula narrat
de consorte suo, cursu festinus anhelo
advolat armenti custos Phoceus Onetor
et “Peleu, Peleu! magnae tibi nuntius adsum
cladis” ait.
sentences.l: While the one begotten from Lucifer tells these marvels about his own sharer, hurrying at a panting run the keeper of the herd, Phocian Onetor, flies up and says: “Peleus, Peleus! I am here for you as messenger of a great disaster.”
sentences.i: While Lucifer's son was telling these wonders about his own brother, the keeper of the herd, Onetor of Phocis, came rushing up at a panting run and cried: “Peleus, Peleus! I am here with news for you of a great disaster.”
sentences.n: Quae ... miracula, “which marvels”, is a connecting relative reaching back over the whole tale just told, with its noun kept inside its own clause. Lucifero genitus, “begotten from Lucifer”, names the speaker only by his father. consors is one who holds a lot in common, so consorte suo is the brother. Peleu is the Greek vocative of Peleus. The genitive magnae ... cladis is split around the line-end: magnae stands three words before the close of its line and cladis is the first word of the next.

sentences.t:
Quodcumque ferat, iubet edere Peleus,
pendet et ipse metu trepidi Trachinius oris.
sentences.l: Whatever he may bring, Peleus bids him bring it out, and the Trachinian himself hangs in fear, of trembling face.
sentences.i: Whatever the news is, Peleus orders it told; and the Trachinian too hangs in suspense, fear in his face.
sentences.n: Quodcumque ferat is subjunctive — “whatever it may be that he brings” — the mood leaving the content still unknown. edere is “to put out”, “to declare”. trepidi oris is a genitive of description attached to Trachinius, “a man of trembling face”. pendet is the verb used of a thing left hanging, and et ipse, “he too”, sets the king's suspense beside Peleus's.

sentences.l: He reports: “I had driven the weary bullocks to the curving shores, when the Sun, highest in the middle of his circuit, was looking back on as much as he saw to be left;
sentences.i: He answers: “I had brought the tired cattle down to the curved shore at the hour when the Sun, at his highest in mid course, looked back on just as much as he saw still ahead of him;
sentences.n: adpuleram keeps the edition's unassimilated spelling, adp- for app-; the same practice gives conligit and Adscendunt further on. cum ... respiceret is a circumstantial cum-clause with the subjunctive, supplying the hour; the pluperfect adpuleram is the main verb and carries the sentence. tantum ... quantum, “as much ... as”, measures the sun's journey against itself — what lies behind him equals what is left, which is to say it is noon.

sentences.t:
parsque boum fulvis genua inclinarat harenis
latarumque iacens campos spectabat aquarum,
pars gradibus tardis illuc errabat et illuc,
nant alii celsoque exstant super aequora collo.
sentences.l: and part of the cattle had bent their knees on the tawny sands and, lying, was gazing at the plains of the broad waters; part with slow steps was wandering here and there; others swim and stand out above the level water with lofty neck.
sentences.i: and some of the cattle had gone down on their knees in the yellow sand and lay watching the plains of the wide water; some drifted this way and that at a slow walk; others are swimming, their necks held high above the surface.
sentences.n: inclinarat is a shortened pluperfect for inclinaverat, the syncopated form verse uses when the -v- syllable drops. genua is a plain accusative object of the verb, “bent their knees”, and not an accusative of respect. The subjects come in three — parsque, pars, alii — and after two imperfects the sentence slips into the present with nant and exstant, so that the last group is still there in front of the eye. campos aquarum, “plains of waters”, gives the sea a field's flatness, and celso collo is an ablative of the manner of the standing out.

sentences.t:
Templa mari subsunt nec marmore clara neque auro,
sed trabibus densis lucoque umbrosa vetusto.
sentences.l: Temples lie below beside the sea, bright neither with marble nor with gold, but shadowy with dense timbers and an ancient grove.
sentences.i: Down by the sea there stands a temple, no marble or gold about it, but dark with close-set timbers and an old grove.
sentences.n: Templa is a poetic plural for one building, and the verb and adjectives are plural to match it. subsunt with the dative mari sets the place low down beside the water. clara and umbrosa are both nominative plurals agreeing with templa — “bright”, with the ablatives of marble and gold denied it, and “shadowy”, with beams and grove granted.

sentences.t:
Nereides Nereusque tenent: hos navita ponti
edidit esse deos, dum retia litore siccat.
sentences.l: The Nereids and Nereus hold it: a sailor of the sea declared these to be gods, while he dries his nets on the shore.
sentences.i: The Nereids and Nereus hold it: a seaman gave out that these were the gods, while he was drying his nets on the beach.
sentences.n: hos esse deos is indirect statement after edidit, “gave out”, “declared”: “that these were the gods”. The present siccat inside the dum-clause is normal after a past main verb — Latin keeps the present for “while” whatever tense stands beside it. tenent, “hold”, is the word used of a god's occupancy of a shrine.

sentences.t:
Iuncta palus huic est, densis obsessa salictis,
quam restagnantis fecit maris unda paludem.
sentences.l: A marsh is joined to this, beset with dense willow-beds, which the wave of the sea standing back over the land made a marsh.
sentences.i: Next to it lies a marsh, hemmed in by thick willows, which the water of the sea, spilling back over the land, made into marsh.
sentences.n: quam ... paludem is a double accusative after fecit, “made it a marsh”, with the noun repeated inside the relative clause although palus already stands outside it, at the head of the sentence. obsessa, “besieged”, is a military word, used here of the willows crowding the water. restagnantis maris is the sea standing back over the land, the participle in the genitive with maris.

sentences.t:
Inde fragore gravi strepitus loca proxima terret
belua vasta, lupus!
sentences.l: From there, with a heavy crash, a din terrifies the nearest places — a huge beast, a wolf!
sentences.i: Out of it, with a heavy crashing, comes a din that terrifies everything near — a monstrous beast, a wolf!
sentences.n: Magnus prints strepitus, a nominative noun, so that the “din” is the subject of terret and belua vasta, lupus follows in apposition, the thing itself named only after the shock has landed. Some editions print strepitans, a participle, “crashing”, which makes the beast the subject from the start. Either way the naming is held back to the end: first a noise, then a huge beast, then the word wolf.

sentences.t:
Udisque paludibus exit,
oblitus et spumis et sparsus sanguine rictus,
fulmineus, rubra suffusus lumina flamma.
sentences.l: And he comes out from the wet marshes, smeared both with foam and, as to his gaping jaws, sprinkled with blood, lightning-like, suffused as to his eyes with red flame.
sentences.i: He comes out of the wet marsh, smeared with foam, his gaping jaws spattered with blood, flashing like lightning, his eyes flooded with red fire.
sentences.n: rictus and lumina are Greek accusatives of respect: the participles sparsus and suffusus are passive, and the accusative names the part affected — “sprinkled as to his jaws”, “suffused as to his eyes”. English turns them into subjects: “his jaws spattered”, “his eyes flooded”. oblitus here is from oblino, “smear”, not from obliviscor, “forget”, whose participle is spelt the same way. fulmineus is “of lightning” — flashing and blasting, not a word for speed. Magnus prints it nominative, of the wolf himself; some editions print fulmineos, which would attach the lightning to lumina, his eyes.

sentences.t:
Qui quamquam saevit pariter rabieque fameque,
acrior est rabie:
sentences.l: And he, although he rages equally both with madness and with hunger, is keener in his madness:
sentences.i: And though madness and hunger drive him alike, he is fiercer in the madness:
sentences.n: Qui opens the sentence as a connecting relative, “and he”. The doubled enclitic, rabieque fameque, is verse's way of saying “both ... and”. acrior est rabie is a comparative with an ablative telling in what respect he is keener, and rabie is the same word that has just stood with saevit for the thing he rages with — the sentence turns on it twice.

sentences.t:
neque enim ieiunia curat
caede boum diramque famem finire, sed omne
vulnerat armentum sternitque hostiliter omne.
sentences.l: for he does not care to end his fastings and his dread hunger with the slaughter of cattle, but he wounds the whole herd and lays the whole low like an enemy.
sentences.i: for he has no thought of ending his fast and his terrible hunger with the killing of cattle: he wounds the whole herd and cuts the whole of it down like an enemy.
sentences.n: curat with an infinitive is “cares to”, “troubles to”, and the two objects of finire, ieiunia and diram famem, stand wide apart with the infinitive's ablative between them; ieiunia is a plural for the one hunger. omne closes one line and its noun armentum stands just inside the next, and then a second omne closes that line too — the same word at both line-ends, once for the wounding and once for the felling. hostiliter, “in the manner of an enemy”, makes this war rather than feeding, which is what the whole sentence has been building to.

sentences.t:
Pars quoque de nobis funesto saucia morsu,
dum defensamus, leto est data.
sentences.l: Part of us too, wounded with the deadly bite, while we defend them, was given to death.
sentences.i: Some of us too, gashed by that deadly bite while we defended the herd, were given over to death.
sentences.n: Pars is singular and takes the singular est data, though it means a number of men, and English has to make it plural. defensamus is the frequentative of defendo, “keep defending”, and stands in the present inside dum although the main verb is past, as Latin regularly does. leto data, “given to death”, has leto in the dative after dare: the men are handed over to it.

sentences.t:
Sanguine litus
undaque prima rubet demugitaeque paludes. —
sentences.l: With blood the shore is red, and the first wave, and the marshes bellowed through.
sentences.i: The shore is red with blood, and the water at its edge, and the marshes are loud from end to end with bellowing.
sentences.n: rubet is singular although three subjects hang on it — litus, unda prima and paludes — taking its number from unda prima, which stands immediately before it. unda prima is the water closest in, the sea's own edge. demugitae is a participle from demugio, “bellow through”: the marshes are not merely noisy but filled from end to end with the cattle's bellowing. The edition prints a full stop and then a dash after paludes; it is shipped as printed, and the dash marks where the herdsman breaks off his report and turns to what must be done.

sentences.t: Sed mora damnosa est, nec res dubitare remittit:
sentences.l: But delay is costly, and the situation does not let one hesitate:
sentences.i: But delay costs us, and the case leaves no room for hesitating:
sentences.n: res is the state of things, the emergency itself, made the subject of remittit, “lets go”, “allows”: the situation gives no leave to hesitate. damnosa is built on damnum, “loss”, and damna, the losses themselves, is the word that opens the account of Peleus three lines further on.

sentences.t:
dum superest aliquid, cuncti coeamus et arma,
arma capessamus coniunctaque tela feramus!”
sentences.l: while something is left, let us all come together, and arms — arms let us seize, and let us bring our weapons joined!”
sentences.i: while anything is still left, let us all come together and take up arms, arms, and carry our weapons in one body!”
sentences.n: coeamus, capessamus and feramus are all hortatory subjunctives, “let us”. arma closes one line and arma opens the next with nothing between them, the shout doubling on itself across the line-end. coniuncta tela, “weapons joined”, means the weapons of men acting together, and picks up cuncti, “all of us”, from the line before.

sentences.t:
Dixerat agrestis; nec Pelea damna movebant,
sed, memor admissi, Nereida conligit orbam
damna sua inferias exstincto mittere Phoco.
sentences.l: The countryman had spoken; and the losses were not moving Peleus, but, mindful of the thing committed, he gathers that the bereaved Nereid is sending these losses of his as offerings to the dead for slain Phocus.
sentences.i: So the herdsman finished; and it was not the losses that moved Peleus — remembering what he had done, he reckons that the bereaved Nereid is sending him these losses as a death-offering to the murdered Phocus.
sentences.n: conligit keeps the edition's unassimilated spelling for colligit, and means here “puts together”, “infers”: what follows is indirect statement, Nereida ... mittere, “that the Nereid is sending”. Pelea and Nereida are both Greek accusatives. memor takes the genitive admissi, admissum being “the thing let in”, “the act committed”: the word names nothing in itself; the dead Phocus at the line's end supplies what the act was, and 267–268 had named it outright — the charge of Phocus with his throat cut. damna sua are the losses just reported, Peleus's own, though the subject of the infinitive is the Nereid. inferias are the gifts owed to the dead, so the slaughtered cattle are read as a payment made to a man who was killed.

sentences.t:
Induere arma viros violentaque sumere tela
rex iubet Oetaeus;
sentences.l: To put on their arms and to take up violent weapons the Oetaean king bids the men;
sentences.i: The king of Oeta orders the men to put on their armour and take up violent weapons;
sentences.n: iubet takes an accusative with infinitives — viros induere, sumere, “bids the men put on, take up” — and the first infinitive opens the sentence, with the verb that governs them, iubet, held over to the next line. induere goes with arma, of armour worn; sumere goes with tela, of weapons carried. rex Oetaeus names the king by his mountain rather than by his name.

sentences.t:
cum quis simul ipse parabat
ire, sed Alcyone coniunx excita tumultu
prosilit et, nondum totos ornata capillos,
disicit hos ipsos, colloque infusa mariti,
mittat ut auxilium sine se, verbisque precatur
et lacrimis, animasque duas ut servet in una.
sentences.l: with whom he himself at the same time was preparing to go, but Alcyone his wife, roused by the uproar, springs out and, not yet adorned as to all her hair, scatters those very hairs, and, poured about her husband's neck, prays with words and with tears that he send help without himself, and that he save two lives in one.
sentences.i: and he was making ready to go with them himself; but Alcyone his wife, startled by the uproar, comes rushing out, her hair not yet finished, and shakes even that loose, and, flung about her husband's neck, begs him with words and with tears to send help without going himself, and to save two lives in the one.
sentences.n: quis is the old form of quibus, so cum quis is “with whom”. totos ... capillos is another Greek accusative of respect, this time after the passive participle ornata, “adorned as to all her hair”, and English must turn it round into “her hair not yet fully done”. infusa is passive in form and reflexive in sense: she pours herself over his neck. Both ut-clauses hold the conjunction back — mittat ut auxilium, with ut second in its clause, and animas duas ut servet, with ut third — a postponement verse allows freely. sine se is “without himself”: the reflexive looks to the subject of mittat, the king, not to Alcyone who is praying. animas duas ... in una is the whole of the plea: her life is inside his, and she is asking him to keep it there.

sentences.t:
Aeacides illi: “Pulchros, regina, piosque
pone metus!
sentences.l: The descendant of Aeacus to her: “Beautiful, queen, and dutiful — lay down your fears!
sentences.i: The Aeacid answered her: “Lay down your fears, queen — beautiful fears, and loyal ones.
sentences.n: Aeacides illi has no verb of speaking at all: “the descendant of Aeacus to her”, with the “said” left out, an ellipsis common at the head of a reply. pulchros and pios are attributive on metus, so the fears themselves are called beautiful and dutiful, and the order to drop them is at the same moment a compliment to them. pone is the plain imperative of pono, “put down”.

sentences.t:
Plena est promissi gratia vestri.
Non placet arma mihi contra nova monstra moveri:
numen adorandum pelagi est.”
sentences.l: The thanks owed to your promise is full. It does not please me that arms be set moving against new monsters: the sea's divinity must be prayed to.”
sentences.i: Your promise has thanks in full already. I do not care to have arms set moving against strange monsters: it is the sea's own power that must be prayed to.”
sentences.n: gratia promissi vestri is the thanks the promise has earned, and it is full before anything has been done. vestri is plural, “of you two”, though only the queen is addressed — the promise is counted as hers and her husband's together. placet is impersonal with the passive infinitive moveri, “it is not pleasing that arms be moved”. adorandum est is a gerundive with est, the construction that states an obligation, “must be prayed to”. monstra are portents, things shown as a sign, before they are monsters in the English sense.

sentences.t:
Erat ardua turris
arce focus summa, fessis loca grata carinis.
sentences.l: There was a steep tower, a fire on its topmost height, a place welcome to weary keels.
sentences.i: There was a high tower with a beacon-fire on its top, a place welcome to weary keels.
sentences.n: focus is a hearth, here the fire kept burning at the tower's top, and arce summa is an ablative of place, “on the topmost height”, with summa doing the work of an English “top of”. loca is again a plural for the one place, and grata takes the dative fessis carinis. carinis, “keels”, is the ship named from one of its parts, and the ships are called weary for the men aboard them.

sentences.t:
Adscendunt illuc stratosque in litore tauros
cum gemitu adspiciunt vastatoremque cruento
ore ferum, longos infectum sanguine villos.
sentences.l: They climb up there and with a groan look at the bulls laid low on the shore, and the ravager, a wild beast with bloodied mouth, stained as to his long shaggy hairs with blood.
sentences.i: They climb up and with a groan look down on the bulls strewn along the shore, and on the destroyer, the wild thing with its bloodied mouth and its long shaggy coat soaked with blood.
sentences.n: longos villos is another Greek accusative of respect, this time after infectum: “stained as to his long shaggy hairs”. stratos, from sterno, is the participle used of bodies laid flat, and answers the sternit of the herdsman's account. Adscendunt and adspiciunt keep the edition's adsc- and adsp- spellings. The beast is named twice in the one phrase, by what it does, vastatorem, “the ravager”, and by what it is, ferum, “the wild thing”.

sentences.l: Then, stretching his hands toward the shores of the open sea, Peleus prays sea-blue Psamathe to end her anger and to bring help;
sentences.i: Then, stretching his hands out toward the shores of the open sea, Peleus prays to dark-blue Psamathe that she end her anger and bring help;
sentences.n: Psamathen is a Greek accusative in -en, and orat takes the person prayed to in the accusative. One ut governs both subjunctives, finiat and ferat, and orat is set down between them, so that the two halves of the prayer stand on either side of the praying. caeruleam is the dark blue-green of sea water.

sentences.t:
nec vocibus illa rogantis
flectitur Aeacidae:
sentences.l: nor is she bent by the words of the descendant of Aeacus, asking:
sentences.i: but she is not bent by the pleading of the Aeacid:
sentences.n: flectitur, “is bent”, is the ordinary word for being moved by entreaty, and vocibus is the ablative of what fails to bend her. rogantis is a present participle agreeing with the genitive Aeacidae, “of the descendant of Aeacus as he asks”, and the two words are split around the line-end, rogantis closing one line and Aeacidae following the verb on the next.

sentences.t:
Thetis hanc pro coniuge supplex
accepit veniam.
sentences.l: Thetis, a suppliant on behalf of her husband, received this pardon.
sentences.i: Thetis received that pardon, pleading for her husband.
sentences.n: hanc veniam, “this pardon”, is the very thing just asked for and refused: what his own voice cannot get, another's can. pro coniuge is “on behalf of her husband”, so the lines make Thetis the wife of the Aeacid who was praying. supplex is an adjective describing how she asked, “as a suppliant”. accepit is “received”, not “won” — the pardon is given to her.

sentences.t:
Sed enim revocatus ab acri
caede lupus perstat, dulcedine sanguinis asper,
donec inhaerentem lacerae cervice iuvencae
marmore mutavit.
sentences.l: But in fact the wolf, called back from the fierce slaughter, stands his ground, made savage by the sweetness of blood, until she changed him into marble as he clung to the neck of a mangled heifer.
sentences.i: But though called off from that fierce killing, the wolf keeps at it, made savage by the sweetness of blood, until she turned him to marble as he hung on the neck of a torn heifer.
sentences.n: Sed enim is “but in fact”, two particles together marking the objection. revocatus, “called back”, is granted and at once overridden by perstat, “he stands his ground”: the pardon reaches him and he does not stop. The subject of mutavit is not expressed. Thetis is the nearest nominative, at 400; the goddess whose anger the prayer asked to have ended is Psamathe at 398, and the change reads as that pardon taking effect. The Latin leaves the choice open. marmore is an ablative of the stuff he is turned into, and inhaerentem, “clinging”, is the accusative object of mutavit, so he is fixed in the act itself. lacerae ... iuvencae is split around cervice, the neck standing inside the words for the torn heifer.

sentences.t:
Corpus praeterque colorem
omnia servavit: lapidis color indicat illum
iam non esse lupum, iam non debere timeri.
sentences.l: The body kept everything except the colour: the stone's colour shows that he is now not a wolf, that he now must not be feared.
sentences.i: The body kept everything but its colour: the colour of the stone shows that he is a wolf no longer, and no longer to be feared.
sentences.n: Corpus is the subject of servavit, and praeter colorem cuts one thing out of the omnia that is kept — shape, stance and the grip on the heifer all stay. indicat governs two indirect statements sharing one subject accusative, illum esse and illum debere, so the stone reports both facts at once. debere timeri is “must be feared” with the infinitive passive. iam non opens the line and begins its second half, the same two words twice for the two things he has stopped being.

sentences.t:
Nec tamen hac profugum consistere Pelea terra
fata sinunt:
sentences.l: Yet the fates do not allow Peleus, a fugitive, to halt in this land:
sentences.i: Even so the fates do not let Peleus, a fugitive, settle in this land:
sentences.n: Pelea is a Greek accusative and the subject of consistere after sinunt, “allow”. hac ... terra is an ablative of the place where he may not stop, with the adjective early in the line and its noun at the line's close, the whole clause held between them. profugum, “put to flight”, describes him and looks straight forward to exul, “exile”, in the next line.

sentences.t:
Magnetas adit vagus exul et illic
sumit ab Haemonio purgamina caedis Acasto.
sentences.l: He goes to the Magnetes, a wandering exile, and there takes from Haemonian Acastus the cleansings of the slaughter.
sentences.i: He goes to the Magnetes, wandering and in exile, and there receives from Acastus of Haemonia the rites that wash off the killing.
sentences.n: Magnetas is a Greek accusative plural, the people taken straight as the goal of adit with no preposition. purgamina caedis are the washings that clear a man of blood he has shed — the killing he was called memor of, the death of Phocus. ab Acasto is the person from whom the cleansing is received, and Haemonio stands early in the line with the name Acasto at the very end, the whole clause held between the adjective and its noun.
